title: Migraine and Tension Headaches
content: Headaches are classified primarily into tension headaches, migraines, and cluster headaches. Tension headaches present as a dull, aching head pain with tightness across the forehead or back of neck, often triggered by stress or dehydration. Migraines present as pulsating or throbbing pain, usually on one side of the head, frequently accompanied by sensitivity to light (photophobia), sensitivity to sound (phonophobia), nausea, or vomiting. Red flags for headaches include sudden severe pain described as a 'thunderclap', head injury, neck stiffness with high fever, confusion, or weakness on one side of the body, which require immediate emergency medical evaluation.
self_care: Rest in a quiet, dark room
Stay hydrated with water
Apply cold or warm compresses to the forehead
Manage stress through relaxation techniques

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome and Cardiac Chest Pain
content: Cardiac chest pain (angina or myocardial infarction/heart attack) commonly presents as pressure, fullness, squeezing, or crushing chest discomfort centered in the mid or left side of the chest. The pain may radiate to the left shoulder, left arm, neck, jaw, back, or epigastrium. Associated symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnea), cold sweats, dizziness, lightheadedness, and nausea. Symptoms requiring immediate call to emergency services (911 or local ER) include persistent chest pressure lasting >5 minutes, radiating discomfort to jaw or arm, severe difficulty breathing, or collapse.
red_flags: chest pressure radiating to arm or jaw
self_care: Call emergency services immediately (911/112/108)
Do not drive yourself to the ER
Rest in a comfortable seated position while awaiting emergency help

title: Upper Respiratory Tract Infections and Influenza
content: Upper respiratory infections (URI), common colds, and seasonal influenza present with nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, sneezing, runny nose, and low to moderate fever. Influenza often has an abrupt onset with high fever, muscle or body aches, fatigue, and dry cough. Most uncomplicated URIs resolve in 7 to 10 days. Warning signs requiring urgent medical care include severe shortness of breath, persistent fever above 103°F (39.4°C) not responding to antipyretics, chest tightness during breathing, or inability to keep fluids down.
self_care: Ensure plenty of rest
Drink warm fluids (water, herbal teas, broth)
Use saline nasal sprays or steam inhalation
Gargle warm salt water for sore throat relief

title: Gastroenteritis and Abdominal Pain
source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
content: Acute viral gastroenteritis (stomach flu) is characterized by watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally low-grade fever. Key focus is preventing dehydration through oral rehydration solutions. Serious signs warranting urgent medical evaluation include severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain (suspected appendicitis), blood in stool or vomit, high fever, severe dehydration (dry mouth, no urination >8 hours, sunken eyes), or intractable pain.
red_flags: inability to retain fluid for 24 hours
self_care: Sip small amounts of oral rehydration solution (ORS)
Avoid milk, caffeine, alcohol, and greasy foods
Eat bland foods like bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast (BRAT diet) when tolerated

title: Cerebrovascular Accident (Stroke)
content: A stroke occurs when blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted or reduced. Symptoms appear suddenly and can be recognized using the BE FAST protocol: Balance loss, Eyesight changes, Facial drooping on one side, Arm weakness or numbness on one side, Speech difficulty or slurred speech, Time to call emergency services. Immediate medical intervention within the golden hour is critical to minimize brain damage.
self_care: Call emergency medical services (911) immediately
Note the exact time symptoms started
Do not give food, drink, or aspirin until evaluated by emergency medical personnel

title: Asthma Exacerbation and Acute Bronchitis
source: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) & Mayo Clinic
content: Asthma exacerbations involve inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to wheezing, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and coughing. Acute bronchitis involves inflammation of the bronchial tubes, often following a cold, causing persistent cough with clear or colored mucus. Red flags include severe breathlessness (inability to speak full sentences), chest retraction during breathing, blue tint to fingernails or lips, or lack of response to quick-relief inhaler.
red_flags: unable to complete a sentence in one breath
self_care: Sit upright comfortably
Use prescribed rescue inhaler (e.g. albuterol) as directed
Avoid asthma triggers like smoke, dust, and cold air

title: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) occur when bacteria enter the urinary system, causing symptoms such as a strong, persistent urge to urinate, a burning sensation during urination (dysuria), cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pelvic pain. Red flags suggesting upper UTI or kidney infection (pyelonephritis) include high fever, severe flank or back pain, chills, nausea, and vomiting, which require prompt prescription antibiotics.
red_flags: flank pain or upper back pain
nausea and vomiting with urinary symptoms
self_care: Drink plenty of water to flush out bacteria
Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and spicy foods
Consult a physician for a urine test and antibiotic evaluation

title: Allergic Reactions and Anaphylaxis
source: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI)
content: Mild allergic reactions present with hives, itchy rash, sneezing, or nasal congestion. Severe systemic allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) are life-threatening emergency events characterized by swelling of lips, tongue, or throat, tightness in chest, severe difficulty breathing, dizziness, rapid drop in blood pressure, or loss of consciousness. Anaphylaxis requires immediate epinephrine administration and emergency care.
red_flags: dizziness or fainting after allergen exposure
urgency_tier: EMERGENCY (if swelling/breathing impaired) / Low (if localized rash)
self_care: Administer epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) immediately if prescribed for severe reaction
Call 911 immediately for severe swelling or breathing trouble
Take antihistamines for mild localized itching/hives as advised by pharmacist

title: Hypoglycemia and Hyperglycemia in Diabetes
content: Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar <70 mg/dL) causes shaking, sweating, fast heart rate, confusion, dizziness, hunger, and blurred vision. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to seizures or loss of consciousness. Hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) manifests as extreme thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and fruity-scented breath (diabetic ketoacidosis warning sign). Red flags include unconsciousness, seizures, persistent confusion, or deep rapid breathing with fruity breath.
red_flags: fruity-smelling breath with deep rapid breathing
self_care: For mild low sugar: consume 15g fast-acting carbs (4 oz juice, glucose tabs)
Recheck blood sugar in 15 minutes
Seek immediate emergency help for severe confusion or unresponsiveness

title: Musculoskeletal Back Strain and Sciatica
source: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)
content: Low back pain is frequently caused by muscle strain or ligament sprain from heavy lifting, sudden movement, or poor posture. Sciatica presents as sharp, shooting pain radiating down the back of the thigh and leg along the sciatic nerve. Red flags requiring urgent emergency care (suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome or spinal infection) include loss of bowel or bladder control, numbness in the groin/saddle area, fever with back pain, or progressive leg weakness.
red_flags: sudden loss of bowel or bladder control
unexplained fever with severe back pain
urgency_tier: Low to EMERGENCY (if Cauda Equina red flags present)
self_care: Maintain gentle movement as tolerated, avoiding bed rest >2 days
Apply ice packs for acute pain (first 48h), followed by gentle heat
Practice ergonomic lifting techniques
